R. S. Furlong Chief Justice H. A. Winter Judge.

maintopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING DIRECT LENDING BY CORPORATION

speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Minister of Public Works):
maintopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING DIRECT LENDING BY CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 2 I informed the house that the government would ask parliament at this session to amend the National Housing Act to extend by two years the expiry date for partial debt cancellation on loans made to municipalities for sewage treatment projects.
Today I should like to make a brief statement concerning the direct lending activities of the federal housing agency, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, under section 40 of the act.
Hon. members are aware that this section authorizes the corporation to make any type of loan that may be made by an approved lender under the act, where in the opinion of the corporation a loan is not available to a satisfactory applicant through an approved lender. The maximum amount of funds authorized for direct lending by the corporation is set by parliamentary vote and on September 29, 1961, parliament increased this amount to $2 billion from $1.5 billion.
Government policy concerning direct lending by the corporation is subject to continuing review, and changes are made from time to time as market conditions and other considerations warrant. Current policy ensures that any creditworthy prospective home owner anywhere in Canada is able to obtain National Housing Act financing for new construction. Furthermore, direct loans by the corporation are also available to builders where the houses have been presold to satisfactory purchasers but loans are not obtainable from approved lenders.
The effect of this policy is twofold. It extends the home ownership facilities of the National Housing Act to all of Canada, and ensures that the corporation's direct lending to builders will not contribute to the creation of a surplus of unsold houses in any community. Including loans to limited dividend companies for the construction of low rental housing projects for families and elderly persons of low income, the corporation financed 23,628 dwelling units in 1961 and an additional 12,761 units up to October 26 of this year.
The house will recall that in October of 1960 special assistance was given to builders in the form of direct loans, not subject to the presale requirement, to permit construction of display houses as an aid to their merchandising programs. A total of 2,215 loans were made for this purpose.
Representations have been made to the government that the special assistance given

to builders in 1960 in the form of direct loans for display houses be repeated this year. The government believes that this step would again be particularly helpful to smaller builders outside the metropolitan areas and would provide additional employment opportunities during the winter months. We are also advised that construction of one or two display houses during the winter months is a most effective aid to builders, since prospective purchasers are thereby given the opportunity to visit sites and examine prototypes of new models.
The government anticipates that demand for loans for the construction of display houses will not exceed 2,000 units. Accordingly, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has been authorized to make two direct loans, not subject to the presale requirement, to any builder anywhere in Canada with respect to applications received prior to January 1, 1963.
It is anticipated that this will be of assistance to builders everywhere, but particularly in smaller communities where the assistance of conventional lending is not as readily available as in the larger communities, and so will be of assistance to employment generally.
I might say, Mr. Speaker, I expect to make a further announcement on housing policy in the near future.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
maintopic: STATEMENT ON STAFF HOLIDAY ON REMEMBRANCE DAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre asked me this question on November 2:
Inquiries of the Ministry In view of the fact that Remembrance day is to be a holiday given to civil servants on November 12, will it also be a holiday for employees of this house?
I have looked over the records of the past since 1947, and I find that parliament has been in session over November 11 only three times. They were in the years 1949, 1951 and 1957. The house sat on November 11 in 1949 and 1957. In 1951 November 11 fell on a Sunday, and the house sat at the usual time on November 12. I therefore take it, on the basis of past experience, that the membership of the house has generally felt that it was quite appropriate that the house should sit on Remembrance day, particularly the day following a Sunday.
As to what the results will be if the house sits on November 12, as I trust it will agree to do following the usual procedure, the full staff of the house will be required on duty. In that case I am informed that there is a general provision for time off for the regular staff of the house in lieu of work performed on days when the public service is given a special holiday.

In this regard I would again refer hon. members to the statement I made some days ago with respect to oral questions. Perhaps if we all reviewed those words we might have a little less discussion now. In any event, in so far as points of order are concerned I would refer hon. gentlemen to Beauchesne, citation 70, paragraph 1, which reads as follows:
Points of order are questions raised with the view of calling attention to any departure from the standing orders or the customary modes of proceeding in debate or in the conduct of legislative business, and may be raised at any time by any member, whether he has previously spoken or not. It should be realized that support of the Speaker in the maintenance of order expedites transaction of business; and the conduct of a disorderly member, if unchecked, may result in an ineffective meeting.
When I read that last sentence I am not in any way indicating that any hon. member has been disorderly. I simply refer to this particular paragraph to make sure that we understand what a point of order is.
The matter of oral questions on orders of the day is not covered by standing order. They are established as the result of a certain practice in this house. I would again refer hon. members to the tradition with respect to these questions which has existed for some considerable time, and which I am endeavouring to follow.
With regard to the point raised by the hon. member for Laurier, I will agree that


within a certain constituency it may be important to that constituency whether the abandonment of certain railway services takes place, but with the greatest respect I am wondering whether the asking for this information at this time of the day is warranted. On that point I suggest that the hon. member might rephrase his question in a general way without argument and we will see what it is like, and I would point out to the hon. member that opinions cannot be advanced in the terms of the question nor should the question seek to raise an argument.

Mr. Chairman, I think the amendment that has been placed before the committee at this time is exceedingly important. Some of us have objected throughout the course of this debate to the words used in the original statute, which said that money would be made available through the Farm Credit Corporation when it provided for an economic unit. There were some of us, this side of the house initially and later followed by the hon. member for Rosthern, who said it would serve the interests of agriculture much better if we said "a more economic unit".
It worked out like this; this is an example. If in the opinion of the Farm Credit Corporation in a certain area it required 300 acres 27507-3-90
Farm Credit Act
of land to have an economic unit, and a farmer had 100 acres and came to apply for a loan to purchase an additional 100 acres, the corporation could then say, "That is not an economic unit, so we will not lend you any money". We believe that such a loan could be in the interests of the farmer, because it would get him along the way; it would improve his position toward obtaining an economic unit.
The minister said there were certain legal objections to the phraseology "a more economic unit". We have no quarrel with this statement of the minister, if that was the opinion of the law officers of the crown. The amendment that has been brought in at this time deletes the words "as an economic unit" and merely says that the Farm Credit Corporation can now lend money-and should lend money, I take it, because this is the provision of the bill-for any purpose that in the judgment of the corporation is necessary for the efficient operation of the mortgaged farm. These are the important words:
-or will increase the value of the farming enterprise in respect of which the loan is to be made.
This is important not only because it will allow loans to be made that otherwise might be turned down, but I suggest it is of very great importance because I am certain it will receive the unanimous support of all hon. members of this committee and in my judgment it is a clear instruction from parliament to the Farm Credit Corporation to lend money to improve the farmers' position, and to lend money to the smaller farmers in particular just so long as the loan will improve the position of the smaller farmers in question.
I consider this an exceedingly important amendment. I feel it justifies the time that has been taken in committee by those on this side of the chamber, and that this should mean, since it is an instruction from parliament to the Farm Credit Corporation, a much more efficient operation of this body in the future -directed to improving the position of agriculture and particularly of the small farmers in this country from one end of the nation to the other. Since we made the suggestion in the first place, we are very happy to support it.

The particular paragraph referred to by the hon. member for Kootenay West is, of course, one of the two main amendments before us. In looking at agriculture as a whole across Canada, and taking into account the experience in other countries, it seemed clear to me, at least, that in many areas of Canada it was impossible for farmers to make a living in what we might call traditional agriculture. It was easy to find other opportunities for making use of their land in ways that are not considered traditional.
The hon. member mentioned recreation. Let me mention an example which I have given before in the house. If one travels down the Okanagan valley in British Columbia and sees the orchards in the fall one realizes the tremendous risk which is being run, the risk that a frost might mean not only the loss of one year's crop but the crops of four or five years ahead until new trees come into production. Mr. Chairman, it would take me considerable time to put before the committee all the various thoughts I have put before the house at one time or another on this subject. If I just list some of the main principles, I think possibly this would suffice. In the first instance, as will be recalled, in my introduction to the Agricultural Rehabilitation and Development Act I made it very clear that agriculture needed some direction so as not to be sent into blind alleys and that the first principle of any redevelopment act should be relating what you are doing in giving an incentive for certain things to the economic return at the end of the road. That principle is inherent in our thinking behind this particular paragraph. For instance, we have made the director of ARDA one of the members of the corporation board. Here you have a man who works with the provinces, who works with all the departments in Ottawa concerning all the resources, sitting on the board of the Farm Credit Corporation. When the various policies of the farm corporation such as the amount or volume of loans going into one particular enterprise as compared to another are under discussion you can have funnelled into that board the best thinking of the provincial government and the federal government departments on the economic possibilities at the end of the road for that type of loan. Hence the relationship between ARDA and the Farm Credit Corporation is very clear.
The Farm Credit Corporation is a businesslike lending operation for long term mortgage credit. ARDA is a planning organization in

which you look at the resources available to agriculture to give higher returns to the farmers. So when an opportunity presents itself, ARDA brings its ideas forward and makes them known to the Farm Credit Corporation so it can follow smoothly behind the over-all thinking of the provincial and federal governments for opportunities for agriculture.
There is a small point in that procedure. Suppose a farmer knows there is an opportunity along a certain road, but this particular path in which he knows there is opportunity does not have immediate returns. A classic example, of course, is the man who is wanting to shift from say a dairy type of production to the beef type of production. He knows there is more money in this new type of production and the ARDA people have indicated to him, or to the Farm Credit Corporation, that the future is good for the next fifteen years in this production. However he says, "I am used to a weekly cheque; how do I live"? This section gives to the Farm Credit Corporation the right to lend money to the farmer during the period of adjustment as part of the loan so that when he gets his income for the year, say two years later if he gets started, he has been able to live during that two years of adjustment. I just use this as an example. There are many other examples of this sort of thing besides the one I have just given with regard to dairy production and beef production.

Mr. Chairman, yesterday I asked the minister if he would give us some indication whether or not in the granting of these loans there were other factors taken into account than merely the efficiency of the farmer who might appeal for a loan. I told him at the time that I am a member for an urban riding, but I certainly make no apology for talking on this subject since I come from the province of British Columbia. lor example, to the United States. Earlier in the debate the hon. member for Essex South referred to the production of frozen foods which are now going abroad to Europe and to the United Kingdom. There is the matter of poultry brought up by the hon. member for Argenteuil-Deux-Montagnes yesterday.

As I understand the past operations of the act, what is proposed by clause 3 of the bill is that there will be a certain charge placed on applicants for farm credit. Of course this is in line with the accepted procedure when one applies for mortgages. Looking at the costs as a whole, part of them are borne by the fees that are charged the applicants and the rest is borne by the treasury of the country. Therefore I would respectfully suggest that it would not be in order for an hon. member to bring in an amendment such as that moved by the hon. member for Assiniboia because it, by setting a limit, means that the treasury has to bear the deficit, and perhaps an even greater share of the costs.
In support of my proposition I refer the committee to Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, fourth edition, at page 214, citation 249, and for the purposes of my argument I refer to subparagraph (1) of that citation in which Dr. Beauchesne is quoting Bourinot:
"No cases can be found of any private member in the Canadian commons receiving the authority of the crown, through a minister, to propose a motion involving the expenditure of public money. No principle is better understood than the constitutional obligation that rests upon the executive government, of alone initiating measures imposing charges upon the public exchequer."
Then there is cited a particular case in the English House of Commons, and it continues:
"On one occasion, in the English commons, the consent of the crown was given to certain formal resolutions proposed by a private member with reference to charges in courts of law to be defrayed out of the consolidated fund. It was thought, however, that any resolution placing a charge on the consolidated fund should be moved by a minister of the crown, and the more regular procedure was thereupon carried out. It was distinctly affirmed, however, that the member who proposed the motion involving the charge was within his right when he had the sanction of the crown, but it was generally admitted at the same time that it was better, as a matter of policy, that the proposition should emanate from a responsible adviser of the sovereign."

Perhaps we should hear from the Minister of Agriculture just what the effect of the amendment would be, but as I understand it, the hon. member for Assiniboia is saying in effect that the crown may be required to pay a greater portion of these expenses.

CORRESPONDENCE RESPECTING SURCHARGE ORDER IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
That an humble address be presented to His Excellency praying that he will cause to be laid before this house copies of correspondence or any documents exchanged between the Prime Minister or the Minister of Finance or any other minister of the crown and officers of the Department of Justice or the privy council or any other government department or agency on the subject of surcharge and imports order, P.C. 1962-902, dated June 24, 1962, and the amendment to the surcharge and imports order, P.C. 1962-987, dated July 11, 1962, and the import control list as amended by P.C. 1962-903, dated June 24, 1962, with particular reference to the legality of such orders.
He said: Mr. Speaker, my motion has to do with the production of the opinion of the law officers of the crown on the legality of the government's austerity program, and more particularly the legality of the surcharges on imports order in council. In connection with this matter the minister had three courses open to him. He could have produced the information for which I asked. This he has refused to do up to now at any rate. I must remind him however that under similar circumstances in 1947, with regard to the emergency program of that year, he asked for the production of a legal opinion by the deputy attorney general. Alternatively, he could have refused to produce the legal opinion for which I am asking. This he has not done. Instead, he is proceeding, and with my concurrence, under standing order 47, making what was a non-debatable motion into a debatable one.
I assume that there can be no doubt that the opinion for which I am asking was written as well perhaps as oral. My authority for this is to be found in the exchanges between the Prime Minister and myself as reported at page 349 of Hansard for this session and as well at page 293. I pass over this phase of my argument with no more than the mere mention of these pages, as J am not receiving

Correspondence on Surcharges from the minister any indication that this statement is an inaccurate one. Anticipating an argument that may be made by the Minister of Justice may I say this. It is a matter of record that he agrees that the opinion received by Mr. Abbott in 1947 was an oral one.
Apart altogether from the precedents on which I am relying in this motion, I remind the house and the Minister of Justice in particular of the position which he himself took regarding solicitation of a legal opinion by the law officers of the crown on the emergency program of 1947. In that connection, as will be found in volume 1 of Hansard for 1948 at page 393, the minister stated as follows:
An opinion of the law officers of the crown has been referred to. I have the greatest respect for the law officers of the crown. I wish to make it clear that I would not be so bold or presumptuous as to set any opinion of mine against theirs; but it would be, I think, in a situation of this kind, extremely interesting for the house to see what that opinion is. In fairness to the house, the government ought to make public that opinion; it ought to bring it down in this house. We should know what the opinion of the law officers of the crown is upon which the government purport to justify this legislation.
Mr. Abbott's reply was, of course, that he could not produce it-

My hon. friends laugh. However, I think they cannot understand what has been said or they would not laugh. Of course I agreed with it. That is the whole case I am making here today. We say that this austerity program of this government imposing $200 million of taxes has no legal foundation whatsoever. We say that no authority is given to the executive of this country to impose this taxation with or without reference to parliament. We say that there is no legal basis for this executive action. The Minister of Justice says there is a legal basis. He says, "We have an opinion of the deputy attorney general". We ask him to produce the legal opinion. We contend that the opinion cannot be that the legislation on which the government based its executive authority had any legal foundation at all. We say that the Customs Tariff and the Financial Administration Act do not contain authority from parliament to the governor in council to enable the latter to make the two orders which make up the surcharge on imports order.
Also, Mr. Speaker, as you know-and I am saying this in passing because it is not essential to the argument as Your Honour clearly understands, I gather from Mr. Speaker's present posture-even if the surcharge on imports order was legal, and even if there is an opinion from the law officers of the crown to that effect, we say that this government should have come into parliament and should have asked parliament to ratify that program or to reject it. We say that we should not be treated in this unconstitutional way by this government. We say that even in this ex post facto manner the government ought to give us a chance of being what we will not be, mere rubber stamps. We ought at least

to have experience with the formality of decision with respect to this illegal legislation.
There is ample authority for the request we are making, Mr. Speaker. I would remind the house that in the spring of 1935 the then minister of justice, Hon. Mr. Guthrie, had no hesitation and without prodding in respect of a public bill as opposed to one involving private rights, to give parliament the opinion of the law officers of the crown. Not only did he give without any prodding the opinion of the law officers of the crown but as well he volunteered opinions on the very point in issue which had been tendered by two eminent counsel, namely Mr. W. N. Tilley, K.C. and Mr. Aime Geoffrion, K.C., on the very point. Those opinions are now to be found in Hansard for 1935, volume 3, at page 3166.
Then in the month of June-I think it was in June, 1935, to be precise-the same minister of justice, with regard to a Criminal Code amendment, volunteered an opinion which the deputy attorney general had sought, again from Mr. Aime Geoffrion, K.C. That legal opinion with regard to a public act, as opposed to a bill involving private rights and obligations, was tabled without any prodding by any member of the house at that time. This opinion will be found in Hansard for 1935, volume 4, at pages 3476 and 3477.
We have, of course, other authorities. We have the authority of May who at page 460 says:
A minister ... is not at liberty to read or quote from a dispatch or other state paper not before the house, unless he be prepared to lay it upon the table.
I argue analogically, Mr. Speaker, that the exchanges between the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fleming) and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and the exchanges between the Minister of Justice and myself put the minister exactly in the position envisaged by May because the minister did speak of a legal opinion. He identified the source of that legal opinion, namely, the deputy attorney general. I submit that having done so he is obliged under the rules to produce the legal opinion, having already gone as far as he has in the identification I have just mentioned.
But we have as perhaps the most recent precedent in this house the action taken by Mr. St. Laurent when he was minister of justice. In May of 1942 the hon. member for Huron (Mr. Cardiff), and the present member for that constituency, moved for a copy of all opinions rendered by the Department of Justice with reference to the power of the governor in council under the War Measures Act to conscript men for service in any theatre of war. That motion will be found in Hansard for 1942, volume 3, at page 2290.
I have in my hand now the actual opinion.

Here was an order of the house directing the government of the day to table an order in council during wartime with regard to important implications arising out of the War Measures Act and the measure for conscription of manpower. Mr. St. Laurent tabled those opinions. The documents consist not only of the order but of the request made by the Clerk of the Privy Council to the deputy attorney general. There is also the reply of the deputy attorney general to the Clerk of the Privy Council and a letter from the deputy attorney general to a minister of crown, the then minister of national defence. That was in wartime; and while we are now dealing with an emergency matter we are dealing with an emergency matter in peacetime.
The Minister of Justice certainly cannot go behind this precedent. He cannot say it is a well known rule that this is a privileged position which ministers of the crown may take. There are certain legal opinions which are privileged, involving diplomacy. Those involve matters having to do with the formulation or execution of foreign policy. But certainly both the precedents in this house and the acts of ministers of the crown with regard to particular requests of this kind are very clear.
I submit to the Minister of Justice that to deny this information is to add to the suspicion that there is in fact no written opinion at all, and creates an undesirable situation.
I am not trying to place my opinion against that of the deputy attorney general. But I cannot believe that in the face of the provisions of the two acts governing this situation any serious lawyer would contend that the course taken by the government has any legal foundation. In the absence of this we must assert that the government has made a mockery of its own bill of rights.

Let me come particularly to the question of the production of legal opinions rendered by those who are called law officers of the crown. Let me make this observation first, that strictly this expression, when used in the United Kingdom today, means the attorney
[Mr. Fleming (Eglinton) .1

general and the solicitor general although in practice, at least up until the last quarter of the nineteenth century, this expression as used in the House of Commons in Westminster, usually referred to the senior officials of those departments. Strictly speaking, if we were to follow the strict interpretation of the phrase, we would take it to refer to the Attorney General of Canada, but in this house we use this expression to mean the senior officials of the Department of Justice and usually the deputy minister of justice who is the deputy attorney general of Canada.
Let us here confine and direct our attention particularly to what is asked for. It is a well established rule in this house that the minister of justice does not furnish legal opinions in the house, although he is sometimes asked to, but this motion concerns the production in this house of the opinions of the law officers, the officials of the department.
Here, Mr. Speaker, we have the plainest kind of statement in Todd, the second edition, volume 1, page 576, where the general rule is thus authoritatively stated:
But it is not the practice of either house of parliament, as a general rule, to ask for copies of legal opinions given by the law officers of the crown to the executive government (or furnished to a public corporation), or cases submitted to the law officers for their opinion, nor is it customary for government to communicate them to parliament should they be applied for. A similar doctrine was laid down in Lower Canada, as appears by the reply of His Excellency Governor Gosford to an address of the house of assembly, on December 11, 1835, for copies of legal opinions, where he states that such communications were ''confidential", and "except in peculiar cases, should be held sacred." They are considered as confidential.
But it is not even usual for a minister to state to the house the substance of an opinion given by the crown law officers; though this may be done at the discretion of the government.
That is what I gave to the house, Mr. Speaker, the substance of the opinion. Campion, third edition, referring to the law officers' opinions says at page 197:
These opinions, being confidential, are usually not laid on the table or cited in debate, and their production cannot be demanded as of right but a Minister is not debarred from citing them if he chooses.
Again in May's Parliamentary Practice sixteenth edition page 273, there is this:
The opinions of the law officers of the crown, given for the guidance of ministers, in any question of diplomacy or state policy, being included in the class of confidential documents, have generally been withheld from parliament.
This is an opinion in the class of confidential documents relating to state policy.

There are so many precedents on the subject, and as my time is limited I must necessarily be selective in the treatment of these citations, of which there are so many available.
Let me first of all take one from the Westminster Hansard for March 4,	1869
where Lord Cairns made a comment as follows:
The noble Earl was about to take a course so unusual-
In this case a minister of the crown was about to read an opinion and he took objection because he said it was without precedent to read an opinion given by law officers of the crown to their governments. The quotation continues:
-and in his experience without precedent, of reading the opinion given by the law officers of the crown to their governments had always been held to be sacred communications, never to be divulged to the public.
The Earl of Clarendon said he had only intended to read the substance of the opinion.
This follows in Hansard.
Lord Cairns must say the noble Earl took rather a peculiar view of what was private and confidential if he considered that he was entitled to communicate the substance of the opinion, provided only that the words of the opinion were not conveyed to the public. With one exception, where a protest was made that it should not be drawn into a precedent, the opinion of the law officers of the crown had always been considered sacred and not to be divulged.
There was further discussion on that occasion to precisely the same effect. Then on June 10, 1870, at Westminster, the attorney general of that day said in debate in the house, as recorded in Hansard:
He must say that, as a rule, it was not very convenient to publish the opinions of the law officers, who are, in fact, private and confidential advisers of the government. They gave their advice on dry questions of law and not of policy; and the government having received their opinion decided whether they would act upon it either to the full or to a modified extent. He had always understood it to be the rule that these opinions should not be published;-
Again on August 15, 1871, we have this statement from a minister;
Under these circumstances, I shall not feel justified in making what I conceive to be an entirely new and objectionable precedent by laying as a parliamentary paper on the table of the house the opinions which are now asked for.
My final citation from the Westminster Hansard is dated April 17, 1877, where the chancellor of the exchequer said:
-he took the opinion of the law officers; but he never promised to lay that opinion on the table, nor could he have done so, because it was an invariable rule that the opinions of the law officers were treated as confidential.
On the same occasion the attorney general said:
He protested against the principle that hon. members should ask for the opinions of the law officers of the crown, not for the sake of the law officers, but for the sake of the government. The law officers of the crown advised the government confidentially; and if the government yielded and granted the papers asked for, similar applications would be made in every case.
The rule is perfectly clear.

The Minister of Justice (Mr. Fleming), I suggest, instead of quoting precedents of the last century and instead of relying on the fact that the hon. member's motion may be a little wider than it needs to be, if he has respect for the rights of parliament, should have offered to give to this House of Commons the opinion upon which the government made the decision that it had the right to pass this order in council. It should not have been necessary for any hon. member of this house to make a notice of motion for the production of papers in order to get this document.
Everyone knows there is a dispute over the legality of the order in council which we are discussing. I have not time and I would 

transgress the rules if I went into it at any length, but may I simply say that I have done a good deal of research into this matter and I am satisfied that the Customs Tariff Act does not give the government this authority. Mr. Speaker, if you will be patient and listen for a moment or two you will realize that I am on the point as to whether or not this document should be produced. It is my view that the Customs Tariff Act does not give the government blanket authority to raise import duties, and on that score this order is illegal.
It is also my opinion that the Financial Administration Act is for the administration of the finances of the country, and that the section that has to do with the remission of individual items does not give authority for a blanket remission. I say that what the government has done is invalid. There are other opinions, but that is exactly the point. There is a sharp cleavage, there is a difference of opinion. The government asserts that its order in council is valid; some of us assert that it is not valid.
To clear up this uncertainty, I requested that the matter be referred to the Supreme Court of Canada for an opinion. The Prime Minister refused to do that. The Minister of Justice said four or five times in his remarks today that he gave the house the substance of the opinion of the deputy attorney general. He did no such thing. He merely told us that the deputy attorney general said it was all right, and that if we disagree with the deputy attorney general we are casting reflections on him, or something like that. I would say that in fairness to the deputy attorney general as well as to himself and to the rights of parliament, whatever the substance of that opinion was, as an answer to the arguments that others of us are putting forward, it should be laid before parliament.
In this discussion we have had nothing but argument by assertion. The Prime Minister says he will not refer the matter to the Supreme Court of Canada because there is no uncertainty about it. Who says so? Just the Prime Minister. The Minister of Justice says he has given the substance of that opinion. One can read all the quotations from the minister to which he has referred. All they state is that the government acted on the best advice, that the government acted on the advice of the deputy attorney general. But at no point in the discussion of this matter has the government told us what arguments there were that gave the government the view that it had the authority under the Customs Tariff Act or the Financial Administration Act to pass this dubious order in council which has the effect of raising

charges on the one hand and lowering them on the other and, in effect, imposing taxes without due process of law.
I was able to get one document from the minister that has some slight bearing on this question. It is sessional paper No. 199A tabled on November 7 in response to a motion of mine that asked for a copy of the order which had on it, or attached to it in some way, something to indicate that this order had been examined to ascertain whether or not it met the terms of the Canadian Bill of Rights. I asked for this document because the Canadian Bill of Rights has in it a phrase -I am just quoting from memory-that says persons are protected from their property being taken away without due process of law.
It is our contention that $200 million is being charged to the Canadian people in this fiscal year without due process of law and I wanted to know whether this had been looked at in the light of the Canadian Bill of Rights. The document was tabled. As I say, it was sessional paper No. 199A. It is a photostatic copy of the enacting portion of the order in council, and at the bottom of the page there has been affixed, I presume by rubber stamp-what I have is a photostatic copy-a notation which says, "Examined as required by Canadian Bill of Rights". It is signed "E. A. Driedger, deputy minister of justice" and it is dated June 23, 1962.

Yes, I said the Minister of Justice produced this document in response to a motion of mine. This is evidence of the fact that the order has been looked at. I think the way the Canadian Bill of Rights operates in this respect is pretty thin, but at least the order has been looked at. Here is evidence that Mr. Driedger is of the opinion that this order in council does not contravene the section of the Canadian Bill of Rights which says there cannot be taxation without due process of law. This is the whole point. We think there has been taxation without due process of law, and no argument in favour of the government's right to do what it did has been given to the House of Commons. I think the Minister of Justice should rise and withdraw his request that parliament refuse to support the motion now before us. I think he should say that he will table the required document without any further request being made. If he has not a written opinion, let him give us a digest of the oral opinion. The minister should not just say he has given the substance of it, when he has not.
Correspondence on Surcharges
As far as the terms of the motion made by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) are concerned, it was just a debating point when the Minister of Justice said it was too wide. How many times have ministers of the crown risen, in response to these motions, and said they are too wide, but if we restrict them to such and such they will produce them, and Mr. Speaker says that the motion is passed subject to the reservation made by the minister. If the Minister of Justice had played fair with the house he would have said to the hon. member for Essex East, "You are asking too much, but if all you really want is the part about the legality of the order, I will table that".

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I just point out that that is precisely what I did.

speechtext:
Yes. And then the Speaker would say, "The motion is passed subject to the reservation made by the minister". But the minister hides behind what is perhaps too much verbiage in the motion of the hon. member for Essex East to try and escape giving this information to the house.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that one of the most important principles in the relationship between parliament and the executive is at stake. Whether I am right or wrong is not at issue. I hold one opinion and others hold another. The whole question as to whether or not there has been taxation without due process of law, whether parliament has been by-passed, whether the executive has exceeded its authority, whether the government has simply done what it could get away with, is before us right now. There are some historic incidents connected with this principle-do not forget King John and Charles I-and that is why I say it is extremely important. I am keeping one eye on the clock; I do not want to talk this out; I want to give the minister time to change his mind and give this information to the house.
I appeal to him. I remind him of the days when we were both sitting on the other side of the house pleading for consideration of the rights of parliament. One of the supreme rights of parliament is control over the imposition of taxation. Here, taxation has been imposed by executive order, by an order in council which many of us feel was invalid. Authority was not sought from parliament in any shape or form, nor has parliament been given an opportunity to confirm what was done. This is a case of executive action exceeding executive authority. This is a case of a denial of the rights of parliament. The answer given to us is the answer we used to get from another source: "Who can stop us?" It is time the Minister of Finance was

In the meantime, Mr. Speaker, this cloak of secrecy is, I suggest, contempt for the rights of parliament.

speakeroldname: Hon. Leon Balcer (Minisier of Transport) moved:
maintopic: RAILWAYS, AIR LINES AND SHIPPING ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMITTEE ON RAILWAYS, AIR LINES AND SHIPPING OWNED AND CONTROLLED BY THE GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
That a sessional committee on railways, air lines and shipping owned and controlled by the government be appointed to consider the accounts, estimates and bills relating to the Canadian National Railways, the Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships, and Trans-Canada Air Lines, saving always the powers of the committee of supply in relation to the voting of public moneys, and that the said committee be empowered to send for persons, papers and records, and to report from time to time, and that notwithstanding standing order 67 in relation to the limitation of the number of members, the said committee shall consist of 26 members.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this motion is to appoint the committee which sits annually to review the affairs of the Canadian National Railways and Trans-Canada Air Lines. This committee has served a very useful purpose in the past, and I am sure the work of this year's committee will prove to be of equal value.
The committee will have before it the annual reports of the two crown corporations for 1961, the auditor's reports on the two companies as well as the budget for each for 1962. These documents were all tabled during the last session of parliament and if this motion meets with the approval of the house I propose to ask leave formally to refer them to the committee together with the usual items of estimates.
Railways, Air Lines and Shipping
The house will have noted that the motion includes the Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships. During the years when this company was under the management of the Canadian National it was the practice to include it in the committee's terms of reference. As the house knows, the company ceased shipping operations, and consequently arrangements were made in 1959 to transfer the corporate management to the government. The remaining functions of the company are primarily of an administrative and financial nature of direct concern to the Department of Finance and the Department of Transport, and the present directors are Mr. H. R. Balls, comptroller of the treasury; Mr. C. S. Booth, assistant deputy minister of transport; Mr. C. M. Isbister, assistant deputy minister of finance; and Mr. A. Watson, chairman of the Canadian maritime commission.
The company continues to make an annual report to parliament, and its 1961 report was tabled on March 21, 1962. As the company no longer comes under the control of the Canadian National Railways, its annual report should not be referred to this committee, and I propose to move that the motion be amended accordingly. In this connection I might add that the motion which appointed the committee in 1961 did not include the West Indies Steamships.
If discussion of the company is desired, an opportunity will be given when the estimates of the Department of Transport are before the house.
By leave, Mr. Speaker, I wish to move: That the motion be amended by deleting the words "the Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships".
Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: RAILWAYS, AIR LINES AND SHIPPING ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMITTEE ON RAILWAYS, AIR LINES AND SHIPPING OWNED AND CONTROLLED BY THE GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not surprising to me that the minister would move to amend this motion, particularly having regard to the fact that the Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships has been out of existence now for many years. It is also surprising that the minister would not come into the house with the resolution to set up this committee properly drafted in the first instance. However, that situation happened once before and the minister knows with what result. In any event, I did not rise to deal with that aspect of the matter. I rose to say to you, Mr. Speaker, that this is the usual resolution which comes before the house to establish the sessional committee on railways, air lines and shipping owned and controlled by the government.
It has been the practice to deal generally and not specifically with some of the matters that are likely to come before the committee. I have no intention of spending any great

Railways, Air Lines and Shipping length of time on this matter as I think the sooner we get into the committee and listen to the evidence of the chairman of the Canadian National Railways on matters affecting his line and of the president of Trans-Canada Air Lines on matter affecting these crown corporations, the better it will be. However, I cannot resist the temptation of saying that I take it there will be discussed in the committee the policy of Trans-Canada Air Lines and of the Canadian National Railways; I refer to the policy of T.C.A. with reference to its own operations and that of the Canadian National Railways with reference to its many lines. Of course, that raises the questions we asked yesterday on the orders of the day and again today indicating that it is high time the government of this country would come forward with a clearcut civil aviation policy in which Trans-Canada Air Lines is particularly interested. I need hardly tell the house that it comes as no surprise to those of us who sit here that an important official of the Department of Transport, no less than the chairman of the air transport board, would make the statement attributed to him in the press of November 7 in which he complained strongly about the lack of policy in that field.
There are a number of matters that come to mind when one discusses the establishment of this committee. When will the government make a policy announcement with reference to civil aviation? I think the time is long past when this should have been done. There have been, of course, contradictory statements, one made at Timmins by the minister's predecessor that there would be no interference in international air routes and another made by the minister himself when he announced a new route for C.P.A. almost a year and a half ago, although authority for landing rights in London for C.P.A. is still not forthcoming.
There is the very vital question of the bilateral air agreements which I sought to bring up today, which are of tremendous importance to T.C.A. and C.P.A. and about which I trust there will be some discussion in the committee. It is very difficult to understand why three and perhaps four foreign air lines should have the right to fly from Montreal to Chicago, Montreal to San Francisco and Montreal to Los Angeles while T.C.A. and C.P.A. have not got similar rights. It was attempted during the course of the question period today to say that these are bilateral agreements and that negotiations are going on with our friends and neighbours to the south in order to better our position. That may be so; but as indicated at the time, these rights should never have been given to


foreign carriers before the two lines operating in this country had obtained similar rights from the United States.
There is, of course, the very vital question of the policy of the government with reference to regional air carriers. The minister did say something about that in answer to a question and I trust that the time will come soon when, following the report of the air transport board in that respect, an announcement of policy with reference to the regional carriers will be made. There is no doubt that the position of T.C.A. has been weakened since this government took office. I say that, confident that this is so, particularly when one looks at the financial aspect of the line. In the last two years there has been a substantial deterioration in the profit and loss picture of T.C.A., and I trust that during the sittings of the committee it will be possible to get some further clarification on this point. Again, it is rather difficult for those of us on this side of the house to understand why the minister would rise in his place and announce a new international route for C.P.A. before he had even obtained assurance from the United Kingdom that landing rights could be obtained in that country.
I said at the start that I did not intend to speak for an undue length of time and I will not do so, but there are one or two matters that I think should be mentioned with reference to the railways. Canadian National Railways, like all other railways, have their difficulties in this day and age, but the position of Canadian National Railways is affected tremendously by the royal commission on transportation. I refer, of course, to the Mac-Pherson commission. That commission was established some years ago now and I well remember the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) telling us in no uncertain terms that as soon as the commission had made its report the recommendations would not only be acted upon but applications could be made in due course to the board of transport commissioners. Again today we had an example of how, notwithstanding the statement made by the Prime Minister, applications are being made to the board of transport commissioners for the discontinuance of lines in various parts of the country while on the other hand the royal commission on transportation has recommended that 8,600 miles of railway branch lines be abandoned upon payment of certain subsidies.
I trust that after these long years of study by the royal commission it will be possible to obtain in this house some indication of policy affecting both the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific Railways in regard to the whole subject of freight rates and

freight rate making because, having looked carefully at the recommendations of the royal commission on transportation I am astounded that over a period of 15 years they mean payment by the taxpayers of this country of $715 million in subsidies. In fact, it is even estimated that the subsidies to cover the whole field over that length of time might reach the fantastic sum of $1 billion. I do not know what the government intends to do about these recommendations but I think it should soon give the house some indication of what it intends to do in that regard.
Then there are the very important recommendations concerning the abandonment of the bridge subsidy in northern Ontario as well as the abandonment of the subsidy under the Maritime Freight Rates Act. If the Maritime Freight Rates Act is done away with as suggested in the recommendations and if the bridge subsidy is done away with, there is grave danger that in those areas where the subsidies now operate the inequality in freight rates and in the freight rate structure will be far worse than it is at the present time. I think careful consideration must be given by the government before it brings down legislation on this matter as well as others that, unfortunately, I do not have time to touch upon.
One thing, however, that does impress me tremendously in dealing with Canadian National Railways matters is the terms of reference to the royal commission on transportation which were varied but which can be summarized under two heads: 1. To inquire into the problems relating to railway transportation in Canada; and 2. The possibility of removing or alleviating inequities in the freight rate structure. After having carefully read the volumes of the report of the royal commission on transportation I have grave doubts that either of these two principal purposes has been met, certainly not with the intention that the government had in mind. When the government drafted the order in council I am sure it had in mind exactly what is meant by the wording of this term of reference, but that is not what is happening in the recommendations that are being made by the royal commission. I say respectfully to the minister and to the government that the royal commission has failed to deal with those two principal purposes mentioned in the order in council.
As I read this report, and as I understand it, the failure of the recommendations to remove the alleged inequalities in the present freight structure, and the danger that that will create, leads me to believe that the inequities which will follow might be greater than those which exist at the present time. While these subsidies are fantastic in amount, there is no
Railways, Air Lines and Shipping condition laid down that these will be paid in substitution for some of the inequities that exist at the present time. The recommendations regarding freight rates, I submit with respect, are impractical in their application, unless of course the well tried principles of transportation law are to be disregarded entirely.
I come back now to the purpose of the motion which is to deal with these matters. I have mentioned about ten of them. There are far more that I could mention, but I do not believe this is the time to deal with them. I think the proper time to deal with them will be either in committee or on the estimates of the Minister of Transport. However, there is certainly a serious problem with reference to inequities in the freight rate structure which it will be expected the president of the Canadian National Railways will be called upon to deal with in committee. I trust that during the course of these discussions, or soon, the minister will be able to give the house some indication when these long awaited recommendations of the royal commission on transportation will be either implemented or ignored, so that the railways will be in a position to estimate their own needs.
I think at the moment of the Freight Rates Reduction Act and the sloppy manner in which the act was handled. I need not tell the minister about that because here we are in the month of November and the Freight Rates Reduction Act expired in April, 1962. There has been no attempt made, either before the last parliament was dissolved or since this one has been initiated, to put that act in conformity with the law. I do not know, therefore, what is happening. What about this Freight Rates Reduction Act, and the 8 per cent in freight rates reductions to which the Canadian National Railway is entitled? How are they to be paid? I do not know what authority there is from this parliament. There is no authority there to pay the railways. Is there an agreement between the government and the railways, notwithstanding the fact the law is not in operation, that the railways will be paid? The house should be told that. Canadian National Railways if it has an agreement with the government as well as the other railways, I am sure would want the country to know about it.
These, sir, are the things that I trust will be discussed in the committee. As I have said, there will certainly not be the slightest objection but, on the contrary, support for the establishment of the committee from this side of the house.

speechtext: Order. I was pleased to see the hon. member was limiting himself to generalities, even though perhaps he did go a little bit further than he himself indicated he might. He indicated the right place where these matters should be discussed, namely, the estimates of the Department of Transport. In other words, we are getting into a debate in anticipation. maintopic: RAILWAYS, AIR LINES AND SHIPPING ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMITTEE ON RAILWAYS, AIR LINES AND SHIPPING OWNED AND CONTROLLED BY THE GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall confine myself to Canadian National and Trans-Canada and, of course, their relations to transportation policies. I agree with the previous speaker, although I would have put it somewhat differently, that this government does not have a coherent policy in either rail transportation, air transportation or any other kind of transportation. This is one of its great weaknesses.
We have before us a motion of which we approve, that is to have the accounts and the management of the Canadian National before a select committee. This occasion, Mr. Speaker, is always one to which some people look forward. In the past, it has provided an opportunity for a review of Canadian National operations and an encounter with Mr. Gordon, if you want to put it that way, for the new members who are interested in this committee. It is a small committee and it meets in the railway committee room. Up until the last meeting of the committee it was a tradition for Mr. Gordon, the president of Canadian National, to answer most of the questions. He would explain the report and the meeting was largely in his hands.
In the past, there have been great numbers of rather distinguished members who have examined and cross-examined him. The list includes the present Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fulton) the postmaster general in the previous parliament, the former member for York West and even the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green) who some years ago had his opportunity of examining the president of Canadian National.
Some of you may be wondering why I am mentioning the president so often. In effect, Mr. Gordon has tended to symbolize Canadian National Railways since 1950. He was reappointed last year after some delay and, if

I understand it, he has three more years to go. He will continue, therefore, to be the symbol of Canadian National and everything embodied in him will go along as it has been for some time. Some years ago some of us asked the government not to reappoint Mr. Gordon. After the last melodramatic committee meeting-someone called it a farce and others might have called it a tragedy-I announced for our party that we were through with this particular technique.
At the last committee meeting, Mr. Gordon came in in a completely different mood, Mr. Speaker. Instead of handling everything himself he had a regular bevy of officials there. We met all the fine chaps who are the senior executives and occupy the administrative positions in Canadian National. My friends across the way will be interested to know that there was not any translation system in the committee room and, as I remember, there was very little French spoken. There are 17 vice presidents of Canadian National and hon. members may be interested in knowing that not one of them is a French Canadian.

maintopic: RAILWAYS, AIR LINES AND SHIPPING ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMITTEE ON RAILWAYS, AIR LINES AND SHIPPING OWNED AND CONTROLLED BY THE GOVERNMENT
speechtext: We know.

maintopic: RAILWAYS, AIR LINES AND SHIPPING ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMITTEE ON RAILWAYS, AIR LINES AND SHIPPING OWNED AND CONTROLLED BY THE GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Anyway, the committee met and we had a performance. It turned out we had an Achilles without a heel, that was Mr. Gordon, and a bunch of heels examining him. Gradually, as a result of the little melodrama injected into the committee, the sympathy of the press gallery members swung to the president of Canadian National and female spectators sniffled. He retired to Montreal with a classic triumph from his melodrama. True blue Don had saved the day against the wicked M.P.'s. Since that time things have been relatively quiet so far as the Canadian National Railways are concerned. Mr. Gordon is still a very pretentious figure.
I should now like to turn to some of the things which I believe should be looked at when we examine the annual report of the C.N.R. Mr. Gordon is a thinking man, a businessman. I have here an announcement carried by the Western Producer of Tuesday, October 4, 1962, when Mr. Gordon went to Winnipeg and called for a master grain handling plan. When one hears that one has visions of grain elevators disappearing, railway branch lines disappearing, and trucks hauling grain all over the prairies.
That report scared stiff a lot of the farmers out west, and it has scared a lot of other people who wonder how far this is going to take the C.N.R. into the trucking business. Just about a year ago Mr. Gaffney, one of

Mr. Gordon's assistants, in a speech to the automotive transport association said:
-I want to make it clear that we have no intention of building anything like a trucking monopoly.
Not the good old C.N.R.-they are not going to get into anything big like trucking. He added:
Our business is railroading, and the Canadian National has too large a capital investment in railroading equipment ever to desert that primary investment.
That may be so, but I have been given some answers to questions I placed on the order paper, which indicate that the Canadian National is becoming a very substantial trucking company, and if this master grain handling plan comes into existence then I can see great fleets of C.N.R. freight trucks ranging all over the west.
This is something which we should inquire into very thoroughly in the committee, and we should seek to find out what projection the C.N.R. has of its entry into the trucking business. In saying this, I am not speaking on behalf of the Canadian trucking association or its associate bodies. To me it seems that association is somewhat demoralized at the present time because so many truckers are waiting around hopefully for big bids for their properties from the C.N.R., and they do not want to take too stiff a stand for a trucking business separated from railway operations.
I want to draw the minister's attention to the situation in his own province. If he reads the publication Quebec Road Transport he will see the issue is very much alive.
My point is that we have a railway which is loaded with debt and which has been borrowing more money to bring its equipment up to date, and its entry on an initial small scale into the trucking business has been developing very quickly. Yet we have been given no idea by the government or the C.N.R. of how far that trend is to continue. I think very good arguments can be made for an integrated transport system that covers the whole spectrum, rail, road, and water, but the way this is proceeding leads me to believe we should be very closely analytical of this aspect of the C.N.R. report, when the time comes.
One of the reasons why my hon. friends across the way may be interested in questioning Mr. Gordon relates to a proposal he made to the government last year that, in effect by a bookkeeping entry or a change in accounts, they could wipe out somewhere between $700 million and $900 million of the C.N.R.'s debt. In other words Mr. Gordon is like the Liberals. He is a debt free advocate,

Mr. Gordon welcomed the report of the royal commission on railway problems, and in the annual report which we will be examining he responded to suggestions made by the commission. The newspapers pitched it this way, and this is from the Gazette of March 21, 1962, "C.N.R. seeks freedom to battle rivals-C.N.R. seeks freedom to fight." So, we find Mr. Gordon, like Mr. Crump of the C.P.R., talking in terms of delight about the MacPherson royal commission. A lot of people have said that the royal commission report with its recommendations relating to the C.N.R. and C.P.R. is, in effect, a document for free enterprise. This is something on which we should examine Mr. Gordon when he appears before the committee.
He wants to be allowed to compete on an all-out basis, but he is the president of an organization that is supported completely and totally by the taxpayers in terms of the capital behind it, and if this all-out competition is allowed, in the free enterprise sector which some hon. members prize so much, then it will certainly have repercussions. Indeed I have wondered about the propriety of the alacrity with which Mr. Gordon was prepared to seize on certain recommendations in the MacPherson commission report. I shall not say more than a few words about it as you, Mr. Speaker, may think it is out of order, but I believe it is a nonsensical report particularly in relation to the Canadian National Railways.
There is another fundamental matter in regard to the C.N.R. which I think should be examined.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very strongly in favour of setting up this committee. I am setting out the reasons why, and the things I want the committee to do. For example, this is from Railway Transport put out by D.B.S., 1961 part VI, employment statistics. I want the house to look at these figures in relation to Canadian National Railways employment performance in 1961. This is the preliminary paragraph:
Railway employment in Canada continued to decline in 1961, dropping 5.4 per cent to an average 166,081 persons from 175,537 in 1960.
Then I miss a few sentences, and it goes on:
The Canadian National Railways employed an average of 92,238 persons during the year under review, a 4.1 per cent decline from 96,227 in 1960.
These drops, Mr. Speaker, in Canadian National Railways employment have not just been concentrated in 1961; this has been happening practically every year since 1955. The situation is that if the projection goes on it will mean that within a 15 year period employment in Canadian National Railways will be almost halved. This involves Canadian National Railways in the big problems of Canada, such as unemployment, automation, retraining, labour relations, and all the rest.
I know how complicated the subject is because I was involved in a dispute between one of the operating brotherhoods of Canadian National Railways and we had briefs piled high before we even got close to getting into the case in detail. One of the things this committee, I would hope, would examine much more closely than it has in the past and really arrive at a much more non-contentious answer as a result of non-contentious questions from its members to the president of Canadian National Railways, who I hope will give a clearer answer than we have had in the past, is the question as to what Canadian National Railways is doing with regard to alternative employment and retraining within its system. We would like to get further into the excuses that Mr. Gordon is always putting forward.
Mr. Speaker, I have so many clippings on Canadian National Railways that I can never plot my way through them, but repeatedly you find statements throughout the year by Mr. Gordon that the demands of labour unions are breaking the Canadian National Railways, or the new demands will mean

the end of the railway. This is probably the way, in our particular kind of society, that the head, the great manager of an organization has to behave.

speechtext: Nobody else overstates their case.

speechtext:
The hon. member interjects and says that nobody else overstates their case. My criticism of Mr. Gordon is not that he is overstating his case in so far as labour problems are concerned; my criticism is that he does not get down to work with these union men who have relationships with his company and try to do something about meeting this challenge of unemployment, retraining and shifting people. I happen to have, Mr. Speaker, as you probably know as a traveller to the west, three Canadian National Railways divisional points in my constituency. What has happened to them in the last few years? Land values have tumbled; people with 35 years work as machinists and skilled tradesmen are out completely. Again, this kind of dislocation is something that we in this committee in the past five years have never really had a thorough, satisfactory answer to. This is one of the things we are going to be looking for, and I hope other hon. members of the house will also.
Having said that, I quite agree that in the past in the committee some of us have been too picayune so far as some of the details we have sought are concerned. I know some of us have actually got down to men working in the roundhouse at various places. But I do feel that this steady decrease in employment, this disappearance of jobs, this impact upon the workers of the Canadian National Railways, is something we must go into in very great detail.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I would like to make some remarks about Trans-Canada Air Lines. They relate partly to the kind of criticism put forward by the hon. member for Laurier. T.C.A. brings to us this year a substantial deficit in relation to its recent performance, and if it goes on as in previous years, we will hear very flatly, very directly, from Mr. Gordon McGregor the reasons for the deficit. As most hon. members probably know, he has expressed his reasons in public very recently. Mr. McConachie, the head of Canadian Pacific Airlines, tosses away these losses of T.C.A. and his own air line, saying it is just part of the jet change. All we know is that T.C.A. was doing very nicely and is now in the red. It is in the red as a result of a government policy change.
Here I would like to make a suggestion in relation to Canadian National Railways, and T.C.A. It is that for a change the Minister
Railways, Air Lines and Shipping of Transport (Mr. Balcer) stays with us in the committee, instead of making his customary presence felt at the beginning only. We are glad to see him. For a while he gives a benign air to things, and then he goes away. I would like to suggest that what we need when T.C.A. comes before us-I know the hon. member for Laurier will agree-is that the minister stay there and when we ask questions in relation to T.C.A.'s performance, the minister should give us some explanation as to why T.C.A. is losing money. If clearly it is as a result of a change in government policy, that is the time we should get our explanations from the minister about T.C.A.'s difficulties.
One of the great problems in relation to air transportation is this. Mr. McGregor told us in one of our previous meetings that despite our population of about 18 million, the core of the people who travel by air numbers roughly 50,000. That is, if you pull these 50,000 people out of using the air line, you just would not have enough to keep many aeroplanes in the air. It seems to me that one of the things we need to get at this time with regard to T.C.A.'s future is how great these deficits are going to be and how long they are going to continue, because it is fairly apparent that this country is putting out a tremendous outlay for air transportation in the sense that we have this huge plant build-up across the country of airports and terminals and all the weather services, radar, and everything else. As hon. members probably know, the Minister of Transport heads about the fastest growing department of them all in terms of staff. It is difficult to use austerity measures in such a department, and one of the reasons is that air lines such as T.C.A. and C.P.A. require a host of built-in services to which the fares collected have no cost relation at all. They do not cover them or come close to it. My argument here is that when we have a relatively small group of our population using an air line such as T.C.A. it seems to me we really deserve a review in this committee of the situation of that company now and in the future, because if the present kind of muddling goes on T.C.A. will not have any future, and it is questionable whether this other enterprise will have one either.
The C.N.R. and Trans-Canada Air Lines are operations which in the past have been labelled as socialist. One of the arguments we often hear when some of us are accused of being socialists is: Look at the C.N.R.- look at the T.C.A. with their deficits. Isn't that an argument against government enterprise? One of my friends after the 1957 election happened to be travelling with the

Railways, Air Lines and Shipping politician who created the Trans-Canada Air Lines, the former member for Port Arthur, and in their conversation the former member for Port Arthur put it very plainly that Canada only had a place for one major air line; there just was not the market or the opportunity for more. Well, this is one case where the present member for Port Arthur and the former member for Port Arthur were in agreement. It seems to me that in relation to both these crown corporations we should not conceive of them as having to be run like a private enterprise concern and show a profit for the taxpayer, but that we announce a policy on public transportation into which the C.N.R. and the T.C.A. must fit in order to give service of the kind required, and then we examine their affairs in order to find out whether they provide such a service efficiently. Some hon. members may suggest I have changed my line compared with what I was saying a few minutes ago about the immense deficits of both the T.C.A. and the C.N.R. This is not so. One can only judge deficits in the light of circumstances in which crown corporations such as these are placed by reason of government policy.
Some of my colleagues have remarks to make in connection with the annual report of the C.N.R. and T.C.A. This is one of the occasions to which those of us who were in the previous parliament look forward-an occasion on which we have a chance to meet two very able gentlemen, because whatever criticism one might direct against the presidents of the C.N.R. and T.C.A., I certainly would be the first to point out that they are men of great ability.

I should like to take advantage of this opportunity to call to the attention of the house the handicap which has been imposed upon the economy of my province, upon Newfoundlanders generally, and upon my own constituency by the recent curtailment of the C.N.R. train services in Newfoundland.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, you will bear with me, because if you rule me out of order there is no other way, as far as I know, in which this matter can be brought before the house or even dealt with in committee. I know from previous experience that when I have sought to raise matters of this kind pertaining to the railway service in Newfoundland in committee, the manager of the C.N.R. has always reminded me that in Newfoundland the C.N.R. is merely an agent of the government because the railway there is not the property of the C.N.R. but the property of the federal government, and the service which is provided is also the responsibility of the government of Canada. Mr. Gordon has reminded me on more than one occasion that when the government says it wants a thing done he is happy to do it, but he does not have to take the initiative himself. You may think, sir, that this is a matter which can be brought up when the estimates of the Department of Transport are before the committee of this house; but on previous occasions when I have brought up these matters on the estimates the minister has said: I know nothing about the C.N.R.; the proper way to deal with this is in the committee.

This is why I should like to bring the question to the attention of the house now, and
I	will be as brief as I can.
Newfoundland has never had a railway
service comparable to that of the other regions of Canada. We have been obliged to put up with a narrow gauge railway with all the discomforts and inconveniences that go with it. I refer to the discomforts and inconveniences that arise from lack of space, small compartments, lack of choice of compartments, and the rougher ride because of the narrow gauge, steeper grades and so on. The situation is bad enough on first class trains but on third class trains in Newfoundland the conditions are almost incredible. The lack of consideration for passengers convenience and comfort is something I believe would not be tolerated in any other part of the civilized world.
In 1949, before we became a part of Canada and when we had a population of only 350,000 and very slim resources, the Newfoundland government operated 12 crossprovince trains per week; that is to say six per week in each direction between Port aux Basques and St. John's. Today when we have a population of 500,000, an increase of 50 per cent, that service has been reduced to 10 or
II	trains per week. The 12 first class trains have been reduced to three first class trains in each direction per week. That is progress in reverse. In addition to that, in order to substitute for the trains that have been taken off, the passengers in Newfoundland are asked to travel on third class trains. A third class train is one made up of a mail car, a baggage car and a freight car with a passenger coach attached. Under normal conditions that train takes from 30 hours to 33 hours to travel from St. John's to Port aux Basques or from Port aux Basques to St. John's. In the winter months when conditions are anything but normal it may take twice as long. The people are asked to travel under those conditions with no sleeping accommodation, no eating accommodation and no restaurants along the route.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to deal very briefly with two points. I am not sure whether I should describe them as items that the committee should consider but which under your ruling might not be admissible or simply say that in themselves they justify this committee, in which case you will therefore accept that they are in order. In any event, I do not intend to do anything more than pick up from where the distinguished gentleman who has just taken his seat left off in his bid for free enterprise in relation to Canada's air traffic. I find this very refreshing when I recall some incidents in British Columbia not so many months ago but I do agree with him. My views as to why we should continue to have freedom of competition between our air line systems are perhaps directly opposed to the argument that has been presented by the hon. member for Laurier when he dealt with the question

of the cost factor and whether or not this government had caused considerable financial disability to the two air lines.
He implied, as did the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher), that since we took office Trans-Canada Air Lines has had some financial difficulty as a result of our policies. I should like to remind him that at the time we took office Trans-Canada Air Lines, in fact every air line, were in the process of converting from piston driven aircraft to the new jets. I can recall certain figures for 1959 when this transition was at its height and similar air line companies were experiencing somewhat of the same problem. For example, KLM lost about $11 million, I believe, because of the transition after having shown a net profit of over $3 million the year before. Eastern Air Lines plunged from a profit position of over $2.8 million to a deficit of something like $11 million. So I think it is significant to point out that both our air lines suffered exactly the same problem in removing slower aircraft. For example, the DC-3 aircraft cost $90,000; the Viscount $600,000. Replacing these with modern aircraft like the DC-8 which is priced clean at about $5 million and equipped at about $8 million was obviously expensive business.
Then, of course, T.C.A. decided to embark on a modernization program. I agree with the view that it was one of the finest air lines in existence so far as air service was concerned but it had been suggested for some years that the line left much to be desired with respect to its ground services. They endeavoured to remedy this by introducing new facilities and new services and these additional costs have had to be borne by them in the last two and a half years. Therefore it follows naturally that these costs showed up in their balance sheets for the last two years and will show for at least the next four to ten years.
The point I want to make is simply this. Surely it must be recognized in Canada that the government's policy of introducing competition has, if nothing else, made Trans-Canada Air Lines a still better air line. I think this has certainly been established to the satisfaction of the Canadian people. We know that dieselization has cost the Canadian National almost half a billion dollars and that this government is now faced with the deficits of the Canadian National Railways.

Mr. Speaker, a few moments ago, the hon. member for Port Arthur spoke of debt free money. Now, in my opinion, if the government had applied our principles a few years back, we would not be faced with large deficits today.
